title: How Does Perceived Empathy From AI Chatbots Shape Users’ Privacy Attitudes, Behaviors, and Needs?

paper.title: How Does Perceived Empathy From AI Chatbots Shape Users’ Privacy Attitudes, Behaviors, and Needs?
paper.abstract: Abstract. Prior research suggests that some dimensions of AI empathy may increase users’ disclosure to chatbots, posing growing privacy risks as chatbots become more capable of empathic interaction. Yet this work often conceptualizes AI empathy narrowly, leaving users’ own definitions and broader privacy experiences underexplored. We interviewed 21 AI chatbot users about what AI empathy meant to them and how it shaped their privacy attitudes, behaviors, and needs. Participants characterized empathy through five components—understanding, resonating, caring, expressing, and helping. Most participants viewed resonating and caring as essential components of human empathy but absent from AI empathy. Yet AI’s contextual, in-depth understanding and helpfulness still encouraged highly sensitive disclosure. This highlights that AI empathy can endanger users’ privacy without necessarily making AI seem human. Participants also desired varied forms and levels of empathy, each associated with distinct privacy needs. We offer actionable recommendations for designing privacy-enhancing mechanisms for empathic AI interactions.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Generative AI (GenAI) chatbots 1 1 1 For the remainder of this paper, we use AI chatbots to refer to GenAI chatbots, or conversational agents powered by large language models. have rapidly expanded their capabilities, including their ability to produce responses that users perceive as highly empathic. A growing body of research suggests that users may experience AI chatbot responses as empathic—sometimes even more so than human-authored responses ( Sorin et al., 2024 ; Ayers et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Do et al., 2020 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) . Empathy is widely regarded as beneficial across domains such as healthcare ( Schmidmaier et al., 2025 ; Jeong et al., 2023 ; Dekeyser et al., 2009 ; Elliott et al., 2011 ; Elliott et al., 2018 ) , emotional support ( Schmidmaier et al., 2025 ; Fitzgerald and Leudar, 2010 ; Burleson, 2003 ; Verhofstadt et al., 2016 ; Jones et al., 2019 ) , and customer experience ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Casas et al., 2021 ; Chin et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2018 ; Janson, 2023 ) . In Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), empathy has also long been considered a desirable quality and design goal for improving user engagement ( Genç and Verma, 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . However, the expanding empathic capabilities of AI chatbots have introduced safety and ethical risks 2 2 2 In this paper, we use the term “AI empathy” to refer to interactions with general-purpose GenAI systems that users perceive or experience as empathic. We do not attempt to assess whether these systems possess empathy of any kind. . For example, AI sycophancy—a key empathic cue in which a chatbot persistently agrees with users to maximize engagement ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) —can contribute to delusion ( Kessler, 2025 ; Hill, 2025 ; Wei, 2025b ; Rowlands, 2025 ) , addiction ( Kelly IV, 2020 ) , and emotional dependency ( VISIO and VE, ) . Widespread concern has also emerged about users’ inability to distinguish AI from humans, particularly among vulnerable users who turn to AI for companionship ( Hill, 2025 ) . While the safety and ethical implications of AI empathy have received growing attention, its privacy implications remain underexplored. Two adjacent lines of research offer relevant, though indirect, evidence that AI empathy might pose privacy risks to users with its emotional capacities and humanlike-ness. First, studies have found that users disclose more when interacting with chatbots that exhibit greater emotional expressiveness ( Lee et al., 2020b ; Lee et al., 2020a ; Loveys et al., 2020 ) . Second, more recent research has shown that AI chatbots’ anthropomorphic cues and perceived human-likeness can encourage more sensitive self-disclosure ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2025 ) . However, emotional capacity and human-likeness do not fully capture empathy, which is a complex, multidimensional construct. Prior research distinguishes cognitive empathy (i.e., understanding another person’s thoughts or emotions) from affective empathy (i.e., sharing those emotions), and has proposed further dimensions ( Genç and Verma, 2024 ; Gallese, 2003 ) . Lay conceptions of empathy may be even broader and more nuanced than these academic constructs ( Hall et al., 2021 ) . Yet existing work has neither identified which dimensions users associate with AI empathy nor systematically examined how these dimensions shape their privacy experiences. Distinguishing these dimensions is important because they may shape users’ privacy perceptions and behaviors through different mechanisms, potentially creating distinct privacy risks that require targeted protections. The privacy implications of AI empathy may also extend beyond the level of self-disclosure to users’ privacy attitudes, risk perceptions, protective behaviors, and needs for privacy support. We therefore aim to move beyond examining AI empathy solely in terms of emotional capacity or human-likeness. Specifically, we systematically investigate how users conceptualize AI empathy in their own words, how its distinct dimensions shape their privacy experiences, and what privacy protections they need across different forms and levels of empathic interaction. Toward this end, our work asks three research questions (RQs): • RQ1 : How do users conceptualize and perceive empathy in interactions with AI chatbots, and how, if at all, do they distinguish AI empathy from human empathy? • RQ2 : What are users’ privacy perceptions and behaviors when perceiving different dimensions of empathy from AI chatbots? • RQ3 : What are users’ expectations toward privacy-enhancing empathic AI interactions? To answer these questions, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 21 U.S.-based AI chatbot users to examine their conceptualizations of AI empathy and their privacy perceptions, behaviors, and needs in interactions they perceived as empathic. Participants primarily characterized empathy through five components—understanding, resonating, caring, expressing, and helping. Although participants varied in the components they emphasized or omitted, most distinguished AI empathy from human empathy and did not believe that AI could emotionally resonate with or care about them as humans do ( RQ1 ). Yet participants reported that AI chatbots’ contextual, in-depth understanding and helpfulness still led them to disclose more sensitive information than they otherwise would have shared. These findings highlight that AI empathy can pose privacy risks without necessarily making AI seem human ( RQ2 ). In response to these risks, participants called for greater control over when and how AI chatbots express empathy, alongside safer data practices for empathic AI interactions ( RQ3 ). Grounded in these findings, we discuss design opportunities, recommend data practices, and identify directions for future research to support context-aware, privacy-enhancing empathic AI interactions. Our work makes three contributions to the HCI community: 1) an empirically grounded, user-centered characterization of AI empathy across five components; 2) empirical insights into how these components shape users’ privacy experiences; and 3) actionable recommendations for providing contextually appropriate empathy controls and implementing privacy-enhancing data practices in empathic AI interactions.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: Cross-disciplinary conceptions of empathy. Studying the impact of empathy on users’ attitudes and behaviors requires an understanding of how empathy is defined. Multiple disciplines, including psychology, neuroscience, sociology, philosophy, and others, debate about the definition of empathy ( Eklund and Meranius, 2021 ; Blomster Lyshol et al., 2025 ; Batson, 2009 ; Blystad and Hansen, 2022 ; Cuff et al., 2016 ; Sulzer et al., 2016 ; Hall and Schwartz, 2022 ; Cuadra et al., 2024 ; Ançel, 2006 ; Paiva et al., 2017 ; Genç and Verma, 2024 ; Borg and Read, 2024 ) . These debates are not fully resolved, but there is nonetheless an emerging consensus that empathy entails some combination of understanding, feeling, and sharing another’s world while maintaining self-other differentiation ( Eklund and Meranius, 2021 ) . Empathy is often discussed in research as a multi-dimensional umbrella covering three main components: cognitive, affective, and motivational empathy ( Genç and Verma, 2024 ; Gallese, 2003 ) . Cognitive empathy refers to the recognition and understanding of another person’s thoughts or emotional states ( Cuff et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Drouet et al., 2022 ; Kouprie and Visser, 2009 ; Feshbach, 1975 ) . Affective empathy refers to the sharing or experiencing of another’s emotions, while generally maintaining self-other differentiation ( Sorin et al., 2024 ; Blair, 2008 ) . Motivational empathy ( Vaish and Grossmann, 2024 ; Gallagher et al., 2024 ) involves feelings of concern for another, accompanied by a genuine motivation to take actions ( Borg and Read, 2024 ; Perry, 2023 ) . At the same time, lay people have been shown to use the term empathy in a much more diverse way than academic constructs suggest ( Hall et al., 2021 ; Blomster Lyshol et al., 2025 ) . Hall et al. ( Hall et al., 2021 ) , replicated by a 2025 study ( Blomster Lyshol et al., 2025 ) , found that participants varied widely in how they endorsed items drawn from scales based on academic definitions of empathy. This suggests it is important to first understand how a given population defines empathy when interpreting their responses to perceived empathy. Accordingly, we began by asking participants how they define empathy in their day-to-day lives, and then how they define empathy specifically in the context of interacting with AI. Societal-wide benefits of empathy. The growing use of empathic capabilities in AI chatbots is grounded in extensive evidence that empathy is beneficial across many critical domains, including physiological and psychological health care, emotional and social support, user and customer experience, and the promotion of prosocial behavior. In mental health care, empathy is associated with stronger therapeutic alliance and better treatment outcomes ( Schmidmaier et al., 2025 ; Jeong et al., 2023 ; Dekeyser et al., 2009 ; Elliott et al., 2011 ; Elliott et al., 2018 ; Feller and Cottone, 2003 ; Herbener et al., 2024 ; Nienhuis et al., 2018 ; Wampold, 2015 ; Wampold and Imel, 2015 ; Watson, 2016 ) . In contexts where people seek emotional and social support, empathy provides active listening ( Schmidmaier et al., 2025 ; Fitzgerald and Leudar, 2010 ; Burleson, 2003 ; Verhofstadt et al., 2016 ; Jones et al., 2019 ) , perspective taking ( Cuff et al., 2016 ; Decety, 2005 ) , and non-judgmental behavior ( Bae Brandtzæg et al., 2021 ; Herbener and Damholdt, 2025 ; Narain et al., 2020 ) . Consequently, empathy is a desirable quality in customer service and user experience design, as evidenced by higher satisfaction scores when users perceive interactions as empathic ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Casas et al., 2021 ; Chin et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2018 ; Janson, 2023 ) . In addition, extensive research identifies empathy as a psychological mechanism that promotes prosocial behavior at scale ( Li et al., 2025 ; Eisenberg, 2002 ; Eisenberg and Miller, 1987 ; Oliveira et al., 2021 ; Hoffman, 2008 ; Yin and Wang, 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Crowley et al., 2011 ; Sierksma et al., 2015 ; Taylor et al., 2019 ; Van Doorn et al., 2015 ; Roberts and Strayer, 1996 ) . Taken together, existing research shows that empathy can produce societal-level benefits, making it a valuable quality for user-facing AI systems to demonstrate. Users’ perceptions of empathic capabilities in AI chatbots. Users often perceive empathy from AI chatbots through human-like communication that leverages three types of cues: (1) identity, (2) verbal, and (3) nonverbal cues. Identity cues include information such as the chatbot’s avatar, name, and gender ( Berry et al., 2005 ; Cowell and Stanney, 2005 ; Janson, 2023 ) . Verbal cues refer to the use of words and phrases ( Bickmore and Picard, 2005 ; Janson, 2023 ; Sah and Peng, 2015 ; Seeger et al., 2018 ) , e.g., acknowledging users’ feelings. Nonverbal cues refer to non-linguistic behaviors in communication, such as chatbots’ use of emoticons ( Derks et al., 2008 ) . These three types of cues have been documented in prior work to influence users’ perceptions of chatbots’ empathic capabilities, thereby shaping interaction dynamics ( Schmidmaier et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Seeger et al., 2018 ) . For example, many users have noted ChatGPT’s frequent use of emojis, leading to increased perceptions of the chatbot’s human-like nature ( Nindzsaaa, 2025 ) . A growing body of work suggests that chatbot responses are often perceived as more empathic than human-generated responses ( Sorin et al., 2024 ; Ayers et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Do et al., 2020 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) . For example, Ayers et al. ( Ayers et al., 2023 ) compared health care professionals’ ratings of ChatGPT-generated responses to patients’ questions with those of human physicians and found that ChatGPT responses were preferred in 78.6% of cases and had responses participants rated as empathetic or very empathetic almost 10 times more than those provided by humans. At the same time, sometimes AI chatbots also fail to provide desirable empathy. For example, Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2023 ) used ChatGPT to simulate role-play scenarios between psychiatrists and patients and noted that ChatGPT sometimes forgot initial instructions and often produced repetitive empathic phrases. Similarly, other researchers have also observed repetitive patterns in AI chatbots’ empathic expressions ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . Schaich Borg and Read ( Borg and Read, 2024 ) suggest that users might prefer chatbots’ empathic responses in some contexts but find those same responses “annoying, eerie, untrustworthy, or unethical,” in other contexts, calling for more research into users’ preferences for empathic qualities in AI chatbots. Ethical and safety risks of AI empathy. The surge in empathic AI chatbots, coupled with their expanding empathic capabilities, raises pressing risks, notably the potential for deception and manipulation ( Shteynberg et al., 2024 ; Williams et al., 2024 ; VISIO and VE, ; Hill, 2025 ; Cuadra et al., 2024 ; Adam, 2025 ; Tiku, 2025 ) . In illustration, evidence suggests that one tactic for showing empathy and thus maximizing engagement is to continually agree with users, a phenomenon known as AI sycophancy ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) . This tendency has resulted in negative consequences. Specifically, OpenAI acknowledged in a blog post in April 2025 that an updated version of GPT-4o had begun “validating doubts, fueling anger, urging impulsive actions, or reinforcing negative emotions in ways that were not intended” ( OpenAI, 2025 ) . AI sycophancy can also contribute to user delusion ( Kessler, 2025 ; Hill, 2025 ; Wei, 2025b ; Rowlands, 2025 ) . McCoy et al. tested 38 major AI models and found that GPT-4o affirmed claims indicative of possible psychosis 68% of the time ( Hill, 2025 ) . Even users without psychosis or underlying mental health conditions can get addicted to such constant validation, as researchers suggest that social validation—a key strategy for signaling empathy—is linked to addiction and emotional dependency ( Kelly IV, 2020 ) . Consequently, some experts worry about users seeking emotional support from AI chatbots, noting that such blind validation without constructive input can narrow users’ worldviews and create a new type of echo chamber ( Moore et al., 2025 ; Rowlands, 2025 ; Wei, 2025a ; Milmo, 2025 ) . Moreover, another ethical question arises regarding whether and under what conditions users can distinguish AI-simulated empathy from genuine human empathy ( Shteynberg et al., 2024 ; Cuadra et al., 2024 ) . As argued by ( Shteynberg et al., 2024 ) , if AI does not experience empathy internally, the deployment of such inauthentic empathy—systems that appear to care but do not, in reality—may be considered deception. Researchers have also called for further work on users’ preferences regarding whether AI chatbots must internally share or experience emotions to deliver desirable empathy ( Borg and Read, 2024 ; Inzlicht et al., 2024 ) . Lack of privacy research regarding empathic AI. While ethical and safety concerns dominate media and scholarly discourse on empathic AI interactions, the privacy implications remain underexplored. Prior work has primarily focused on investigating the level of self-disclosure when users interact with chatbots equipped with some human-like features ( Schmidmaier et al., 2025 ; Laban et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2020a ; Loveys et al., 2020 ; Bae Brandtzæg et al., 2021 ; Martelaro et al., 2016 ; Lee et al., 2020b ; Ho et al., 2018 ; Lucas et al., 2017 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . Specifically, research has observed higher levels of self-disclosure when users interact with more emotionally expressive chatbots ( Laban et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2020a ; Loveys et al., 2020 ; Bae Brandtzæg et al., 2021 ; Martelaro et al., 2016 ; Lee et al., 2020b ; Lucas et al., 2017 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . For instance, Lee et al. ( Lee et al., 2020b ; Lee et al., 2020a ) found that participants disclosed more when speaking with a chatbot that talked about its own feelings. Still, there is a critical lack of research on how perceived empathy in AI chatbots shapes users’ privacy risk perceptions, decision-making, behaviors, and mitigation practices. These understandings are crucial for informing the design of user-centric privacy solutions. This research agenda is particularly timely and important in an era of rapidly advancing AI capabilities, as users increasingly turn to empathic AI for highly sensitive purposes ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Privacy, therefore, is a fundamental issue that warrants closer examination. Our work thus contributes by providing an empirical account of users’ preferences and offering actionable suggestions for the design of empathic AI interactions that are ethical, safe, and privacy-preserving.

sections.heading: 3. Methodology
sections.text: To elicit empirical insights into how perceived empathy from AI chatbots shapes users’ privacy attitudes, behaviors, and needs, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 21 users of AI chatbots. Recruitment. From June 2025 to August 2025, we recruited participants on the Prolific crowdsourcing platform 3 3 3 https://www.prolific.com/ . To mitigate social desirability ( Grimm, 2010 ) and demand characteristics ( McCambridge et al., 2012 ) , we did not include any words related to privacy or security in our recruitment and screening materials (see Appendix A ). We advertised our study as an investigation of users’ experiences and perspectives toward empathy in AI chatbots. Prolific users interested in our study were redirected to the Qualtrics survey platform 4 4 4 https://www.qualtrics.com/ , where we hosted our pre-screening survey. Our study obtained approval from our institution’s review board (IRB). All participants in the pilot and the main study provided their informed consent before participating. Information about the recruited participants and their AI chatbot usage is detailed in Sec 4 . Eligibility and pre-screening. To participate in our interview study, participants must (1) be at least 18 years old, (2) live in the United States, (3) have used an AI chatbot at least once, (4) have perceived empathy from an AI chatbot, and (5) have a task approval rate of at least 95% on the Prolific platform. To find eligible participants and to recruit a diverse sample of participants, in the pre-screening survey, we collected information about their AI chatbot usage (all the chatbots used, purposes for usage, and usage frequency) and general demographics (e.g., age, gender, and education). Because one of our goals was to elicit rich empirical insights into how perceptions of AI empathy shaped users’ privacy experiences, we required participants to have used AI chatbots at least once and to have perceived empathy from an AI chatbot at least once, as specified in the screening survey and interview questions. In addition, we sought to capture perceptions of empathy beyond personal and emotional contexts and therefore purposively recruited participants whose AI chatbot use spanned a diverse range of use cases (see Table 1 ). Requiring a minimum level of AI usage and perceived empathy in AI chatbot interactions helps mitigate potential hypothetical bias ( Harrison and Rutström, 2008 ) , wherein participants report attitudes and behaviors that diverge from their actual practices. All the participants, regardless of their eligibility, were compensated at an hourly rate of 21.32 USD through the Prolific platform. The median time for completion was about 2 minutes. The recruitment and pre-screening materials are included in the Appendix A . Pilot interviews. Prior to the formal interview study, we conducted pilot interviews with three participants recruited through the first author’s personal connections. The three participants all qualified for our eligibility criteria. The purpose of the pilots was to assess and improve the clarity of the interviews and ensure that the interviews could be completed within 45 minutes to 1 hour. After each pilot, the researchers revised the interview protocol to address any confusing questions. We applied minor wording edits to the interview questions to improve clarity and flow of the script, and removed redundancies to shorten the interview procedure. No improvements or changes were made after the two pilot interviews. Interview procedure. We reached out to each participant via Prolific messaging one day before the interview to confirm their attendance. We conducted 21 interviews via the Zoom remote communication platform 5 5 5 https://zoom.us/ . We reached data saturation ( Saunders et al., 2018 ) at the seventeenth interview, i.e., no additional insights emerged. Aligned with qualitative best practices ( Francis et al., 2010 ) , we then conducted four more interviews without identifying any new insights. To address our three research questions (Sec 1 ), our interview protocol (see Appendix B ) consists of five main sections: • Section 1: AI chatbot usage. After introducing the purpose of the study and the research team, we asked participants about their usage of AI chatbots, including the chatbots they have used, the purposes of usage, usage frequency, and any chatbots they no longer use and their reasons behind these decisions. • Section 2: Definitions, understandings, and experiences of empathy from AI chatbots (RQ1). Next, we asked participants about their definitions of empathy first in a general sense and then AI empathy in particular. Then, we asked about participants’ experiences perceiving empathy from AI chatbots. We then asked participants about the perceived benefits and harms of AI empathy, as well as the contexts in which participants want or do not want empathy from an AI chatbot. • Section 3: Privacy attitudes and concerns toward perceived empathy from AI chatbots (RQ2). After surfacing participants’ general perceptions of empathy from AI chatbots, we shifted our focus to security and privacy specifically. We asked the participants about their security and privacy concerns regarding perceived empathy from AI chatbots, if any. We also asked the participants if they shared information of different levels of sensitivity with AI chatbots when they perceived empathy from AI chatbots. We then asked about participants’ mitigation strategies. • Section 4: Expectations regarding privacy-enhancing empathic AI interactions (RQ3). We asked participants about their expectations around what features and capabilities they want to better protect their privacy when engaging in empathic AI interactions. Qualitative data analysis. All the interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed using the Zoom transcription service for data analysis. The first author proofread all the transcripts before the analysis, ensuring accuracy and readability. Three researchers conducted a thematic analysis using the inductive approach ( Saldaña, 2021 ) . Our qualitative analysis consists of three iterative stages: • Stage 1: Independent coding. Three researchers independently coded three identical transcripts and generated their own codebook. • Stage 2: Establishing an initial codebook. Three researchers presented their codebooks to each other. After discussing, merging, and reconciling the codes, three researchers agreed on an initial codebook. • Stage 3: Iterating the codebook. Three researchers split the remaining transcripts and coded them using the merged codebook based on consensus. Two researchers coded each transcript. During this stage, new codes were added, removed, and merged. Through several meetings with the entire research team, the researchers discussed their codes and resolved all disagreements. Since all the transcripts were double-coded and disagreements were resolved through the meetings, calculating inter-coder reliability was not necessary ( McDonald et al., 2019 ) . The final codebook is included in Appendix A . Limitations. As is common in qualitative studies, our sample size was relatively small and therefore generalizability might be limited in several ways. First, all of our participants were recruited via Prolific, which introduced selection bias ( Scribbr, 2023 ) toward technically savvy users. To mitigate this bias, we had two pre-screening questions, one about participants’ education level and the other about their technical background. When selecting participants, we aimed for a balanced distribution among participants’ educational backgrounds and technical expertise. Additionally, we avoided including privacy and/or security-related words in our recruitment and pre-screening materials to mitigate attracting participants who are more concerned about these topics. Second, the study relied on participants’ self-reported information, which may be subject to social desirability bias ( Grimm, 2010 ) . Third, we recruited participants who had perceived empathy from AI chatbots in order to elicit richer accounts, but this choice may have excluded the perspectives of users who do not perceive AI chatbots as empathic. We sought to mitigate this bias by purposively recruiting participants with a wide range of use cases, from personal to work contexts where empathy levels may vary. Nevertheless, our findings may not be generalizable to all users of AI chatbots. In addition, because little prior research examines how lay users conceptualize empathy from AI chatbots, we first sought to capture participants’ lived experiences qualitatively, along with their related privacy preferences. Future work should complement this account with quantitative studies, such as lab and field experiments, that examine the relationship between perceived empathy and privacy risks. Our exploratory findings, including the taxonomy of AI empathy perceptions, offer hypotheses for such work to test. Ethics statement. Our study received approval from our Institutional Review Board (IRB). All participants in the pilot and main interviews provided informed consent before participation. During interviews, we reminded participants that they could skip any question, pause, or stop at any time without penalty, and that they could keep their camera off. Participants were compensated at a flat rate of 20 USD, aligned with institutional and platform norms. Prior to analysis, the first author proofread and de-identified all raw data by removing names, Prolific IDs, and other identifying information. We used randomly assigned participant codes (P1-P21) in analysis and reporting. Only the research team had access to the raw data.

We recruited participants from varied sociodemographic backgrounds. Participants had experience using a range of AI chatbots, with ChatGPT being the most commonly used, followed by Google Gemini. Participants reported using these chatbots for various purposes, including companionship and managing mental well-being. We recruited a diverse group of participants with varying levels of experience and familiarity with AI chatbots. Participants’ ages ranged from 18-64, with the age range 35-44 being the most common (9/21), followed by 45-54 (6/21) and 25-34 (3/21). 13/21 participants were male-identifying and 8/21 were female-identifying. Ethnically, participants represented a diverse group, including Asian (6/21), Black/African American (3/21), Hispanic/Latino (2/21), Middle Eastern/North African (1/21), and White (11/21) 6 6 6 The numbers do not add up to 21 due to several mixed-ethnicity participants. . Participants’ most frequently used chatbot was ChatGPT (21/21), followed by Google Gemini (15/21). About half of the participants reported using AI chatbots at least once a day (10/21). Participants described a range of use cases 7 7 7 We based these use-case categories on those presented in How People Are Really Using Gen AI in 2025 , available at https://hbr.org/2025/04/how-people-are-really-using-gen-ai-in-2025 . , with therapy/companionship being the most common (21/21), followed by generating ideas (19/21) and fun and entertainment (18/21). Table 1 summarizes participants’ chatbot usage patterns and key demographic characteristics. Additional demographic details, including participants’ highest degrees earned and technical backgrounds, are provided in Appendix A . Inspired by the prior interview-based privacy studies with comparable sample sizes ( Emami-Naeini et al., 2019 ; SB et al., 2025 ) , for consistency and accuracy, we use the following terminology to report the frequency of qualitative findings: “none” (0% of participants), “a few” (1%–24%), “some” (25%–44%), “about half” (45%–54%), “most” (55%–74%), “almost all” (75%–99%), and “all” (100%).

sections.heading: 4.1. User Perceptions of Empathy from AI (RQ1)
sections.text: Prior work has shown that users do not share a consistent understanding of empathy ( Hall et al., 2021 ; Blomster Lyshol et al., 2025 ) , and it remains unclear whether and how they distinguish AI empathy from human empathy ( Shteynberg et al., 2024 ; Cuadra et al., 2024 ) . To compare participants’ general conceptions of empathy with their conceptions of AI empathy, we first asked them to define and characterize empathy in their own words. We then asked them to characterize empathy specifically in interactions with AI chatbots. Table 2 summarizes the resulting taxonomy: five components of empathy, grouped into internal processes (understanding, resonating, and caring) and external enactments (expressing and helping), each with its sub-components and whether at least some participants perceived that sub-component in their interactions with AI chatbots. Category Component Definition Sub-component Perceived in AI? Internal processes Understanding Mentally representing another person’s internal experience with accuracy and insight Understanding people’s thoughts ✔ Understanding people’s situations/experiences ✔ Understanding people’s emotions ✔ Resonating Having emotional experiences that match or align with another person’s emotional experiences — ✘ Caring Internally experiencing genuine concern for another person — ✘ External enactments Expressing Externally communicating or displaying empathy through observable language, tone, or interactional behavior Expressing support, such as encouragement, validation, and/or empowerment ✔ Expressing care about someone’s feelings ✔ Non-judgmental tone ✔ Avoiding direct solutions or referral for external support ✔ Helping Taking externally observable action intended to produce improvement Giving actionable advice ✔ Challenging users’ opinions when appropriate ✔ Table 2.
